headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. State Assembly District 12: Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward compete in a battle between business and labor. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Sonoma County and additional election information, visit the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters website. headlines.title: Sell-off for tech stocks deepens, drags Wall Street toward its worst day since June
headlines.description: A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high. The S&P 500 dropped 1.8% and was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the month. The Nasdaq composite was likewise heading toward its worst day since June, as the weakness for technology stocks dragged it down 3%, as of 12:55 p.m. Eastern time. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 496 points, or 0.9%. Intel’s stock led the way downward and is flirting with its worst day since 1974 after tumbling 30.1%. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Amazon sank 2.3% after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through $42.4 billion of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology. A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12% to its worst day on record and almost single-handedly dragged the S&P 500 lower after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI. Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centers have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers. “We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors. A drop of 4.7% for the stock price of Nvidia, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, even more than Intel. In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6 billion worth of crypto at Binance. Coinbase Global fell 12.9% even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4% of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 6%. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons. Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose in the S&P 500 index as fell. ExxonMobil climbed 1.8%, and Chevron added 1.6% after the oil giants both reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Mondelez International rose 3.7% after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth. Colgate-Palmolive climbed 3.5% after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected. Expectations are high for U.S. companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94% from 4.98% late Thursday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields higher because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4% to $113.50. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Europe following sharper swings in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5% as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1% after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank.

headlines.title: Bay Area real estate executive sentenced to 18 months for defrauding investors
headlines.description: A former Bay Area real estate executive was sentenced earlier this week to 18 months in federal prison for defrauding investors of more than $2.2 million, according to federal prosecutors. Sanjeev Acharya, 58, of San Jose, was sentenced Wednesday for wire fraud and a financial transaction involving money obtained through fraud, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California said in a statement. Acharya was the president and CEO of SiliconSage Builders and related companies, which supported investments in large real estate developments across the Bay Area. He personally solicited investments to fund the projects, according to his plea agreement. Federal prosecutors said Acharya misled more than 20 investors between March and Oct. 26, 2020, by failing to disclose that SiliconSage was heavily in debt and facing serious cash flow problems. The company was struggling financially in part because of the COVID-19 pandemic and needed new investments to stay afloat, according to the plea agreement. The investors lost more than $2.2 million as a result of the fraud, prosecutors said. “Behind these losses are individuals and families whose retirement plans, educational opportunities, and financial security were put at risk,” said John Abram, acting special agent in charge of the IRS Criminal Investigation San Francisco Field Office. Acharya was charged in September 2025 and pleaded guilty in January 2026 to wire fraud and engaging in a monetary transaction involving property derived from fraud. Besides the prison sentence, Breyer ordered Acharya to serve two years of supervised release and pay $2.25 million in restitution to victims. Acharya is scheduled to begin serving his sentence on Jan. 9, 2027.

headlines.title: Coastal flooding expected to continue, rain possible across Bay Area
headlines.description: Moderate coastal flooding is possible along Bay Area shorelines through Sunday, while light rain could reach parts of the region Saturday, according to the National Weather Service. In an advisory early Friday, the weather service warned that high tides could flood low-lying areas, cause isolated road closures and contribute to coastal erosion. Rising water and waves could also reach farther up beaches than usual, making it harder for people to leave coastal areas safely. The coastal flooding risk extends along the shores of San Pablo, San Francisco and Monterey bays, as well as the Pacific coast. At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide is expected to reach 1.9 feet above normal at 2:39 p.m. Friday. The level is forecast to reach 1.5 feet above normal on Saturday afternoon and a foot above normal on Sunday afternoon. At the Monterey tidal gauge, high tide is forecast to reach 1.8 feet above normal at 1:25 p.m. Friday. It is expected to reach 1.4 feet above normal Saturday and 0.8 feet above normal Sunday. The tide forecasts include about 1.5 feet of additional water from surge effects linked to thermal expansion and low pressure. High tide times can vary by as much as 90 minutes along the coast and throughout San Francisco Bay, forecasters said. Rain chances, meanwhile, are projected for Saturday, but the weather service said confidence remains low across much of the region. Most areas have a 10% to 30% chance of Halloween rain, with expected totals ranging from a few hundredths to about a tenth of an inch. Monterey County could see higher rain chances. The interior areas have a 50% to 70% probability of precipitation, while other areas in the two counties have a 30% to 50% chance. Rainfall totals could reach about a tenth to a third of an inch in the interior, forecasters said. The weather service said rain chances could return next week, with seasonal to slightly below seasonal temps expected through the extended forecast. Residents near the coast are advised to allow extra travel time because of possible road closures, avoid driving around barricades or through floodwaters of unknown depth, and take steps to protect property from flooding.

headlines.title: Nakase and Valkyries are determined to avoid another slow start in WNBA Finals Game 7 against Dream
headlines.description: There should be no problem with the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream approaching the first WNBA Finals Game 7 in league history with a sense of urgency. Then again, that’s what Golden State coach Natalie Nakase thought about Game 6. She was baffled that her team somehow left behind its defensive intensity at the start of Thursday’s 80-69 loss to the Dream that forced Game 7 at “Ballhalla” in San Francisco on Saturday night. While the Valkyries were missing their defensive edge that was so important in their 64-55 Game 5 win, the Dream seized the opportunity by making 73.3% of their shots in the first quarter and racing to a 32-15 lead. The 32 points are the most by either team in a quarter in the series. Atlanta kept the lead in double figures most of the remainder of the game. “Can’t let that happen right out of the gate,” Valkyries guard Veronica Burton said. “There needs to be a sense of urgency. It’s the WNBA Finals.” Even after the Valkyries showed fight by attempting a second-half comeback, Nakase was still struggling to comprehend the lackadaisical start so she could make sure it’s not repeated in Saturday night’s decisive game. She said she planned to have conversations with her players about the issue on the flight back to California. “I put that on me of like, what did I not say, what did I not get to my team of the sense of urgency that we knew they were going to play?” Nakase said of the Dream. “We knew they were going to play desperate. We knew they were going to play like their life depends on it. For us not to match that is disappointing and frustrating. So, yeah, I need to make sure my team is prepared.” Added Nakase of her plan to seek answers: “For me, I need clarity. I need some information.” The Dream and Valkyries each will be playing for their first WNBA title. Unfinished business Atlanta’s Allisha Gray scored 23 points and Rhyne Howard had 21 in Thursday’s win when Golden State’s only lead was 2-0. Angel Reese added 15 points and 14 rebounds for the Dream. “Our job is not done,” Reese said. “We definitely could be happy about it for now but we have more work to do. I think we definitely have another level that we can get to, like (Gray) was saying. We shot a lot better this game, for sure, but I think we just continue to grow from this.” A first for the Finals The format for the WNBA Finals was a best-of-five series until the first best-of-seven series in 2025, when the Las Vegas Aces swept the Phoenix Mercury 4-0. The Dream lost in the Finals in 2010, 2011 and 2013. The Valkyries reached this year’s Finals in only their second season of existence. Atlanta fans pack State Farm Arena Despite Thursday’s Game 6 being scheduled for a much-criticized 12:30 p.m. EDT tipoff that created concerns about fans’ obligations to work and school, Atlanta supporters delivered a sellout of 17,099 at State Farm Arena. “Shout out to the crowd, being able to come here at 12:30 on a Thursday and so many things going on in the world from school to work, to everything else,” Reese said. “We’re just super thankful. We fed off their energy. They were loud from the beginning. So we’re definitely thankful for that.” Reese knows another packed house will be supporting the Valkyries on Saturday night. “I think that the crowd doesn’t really get to us much but I think, obviously, Game 7 is going to be a lot louder,” Reese said. “The energy is going to be electric in there. So just honestly staying poised, staying together, and I think we’ll be fine.” Injury scare for Hayes Golden State’s Tiffany Hayes was called for her fifth foul in a collision for a loose ball with 5:01 remaining. Hayes was left laying on the court following the collision. She slowly walked off after receiving attention from a trainer. Nakase said she wanted to check in again with Hayes but added “she looked good to me. Yeah, she looked fine.” Don’t blame the early start Nakase and her players firmly denied the early start — 9:30 a.m. by California time — was a factor in the Valkyries’ slow start. “No. That had nothing to do with it,” Nakase said. “We played at 1 o’clock last week. No.” Added Gabby Williams: “They played at the same time as us, right? So it’s not an excuse. We have to be better.” ___ See AP’s full WNBA coverage here

headlines.title: High tides continue flooding Marin County, filling roads and neighborhoods
headlines.description: Thursday, high tides brought floodwaters onto roads, into parking lots, and through neighborhoods throughout Marin County. Elevated water levels were spotted around the county during and after high tide, just after midday Thursday afternoon. These elevated water levels came on what was otherwise a clear day in Marin County. Video footage from the news chopper from that time showed flooding in Sausalito, Belvedere, Mill Valley, Corte Madera, and more. Forecasters say the high tides are compounded by especially warm waters off the Pacific, with thermal expansion of the water leading water levels to rise. Already, officials warned residents of coastal areas to be on alert for flooding this week. Now, the National Weather Service has extended its Coastal Flood Advisory through Sunday at 6 p.m. for low-lying, bayshore locations along the San Pablo Bay, San Francisco Bay, and Monterey Bay. “It’s a little bit alarming, I live right on the marsh,” said Nancy Miller of Mill Valley, who noticed the water level rising at the marsh outside where she lives this week. “Oh yes, I’ve lived here now 9 years, and it’s definitely more than I’ve ever seen,” she said. The high tide flooding prompted Caltrans to close the ramp that connects northbound Highway 101 and Highway 1 in Mill Valley, explained Matt O’Donnell, Marin County Public Information Officer for Caltrans. “They have had to close that same ramp quite a few times this month,” he noted, adding that with El Niño in the forecast for this winter, residents should stay on alert for more possible road closures. O’Donnell noted that drivers who drive into flooded roads risk their own safety and damage to their cars. “It’s just not worth the risk, if a maintenance worker is telling you to stay off that roadway, then stay off that roadway please,” he emphasized. Thursday, Lucky Drive in Corte Madera off of 101 flooded, as it has been known to do during high tides. Officials blocked off parts of the roadway and directed traffic around some of the deeper areas of water. Mary Sackett, Marin County Supervisor for District 1, which covers San Rafael, explained that county workers have been going door-to-door in the Santa Venetia area, asking for access to properties to do flood prevention work. “We really ask that you say yes, and open your door and allow us to do what we can,” Sackett said.

headlines.title: Half Moon Bay's ballot fight over senior farmworker housing
headlines.description: Candido Rosales spent more than 30 years working at flower farms. In retirement, he is still searching for something he can afford: a home where he, his wife and their daughter can live together. Rosales rents a room. His wife and daughter, who recently arrived from Mexico, stay in a separate home with family. “There’s nowhere to live or for all three of us to live together. It’s very difficult,” he said in Spanish. His struggle is part of the debate over Measure Q, which asks Half Moon Bay voters whether to uphold agreements allowing an affordable housing project for senior agricultural workers on city-owned land near downtown. Supporters say the homes would give aging farmworkers a chance to retire with dignity. Opponents question whether the five-story development is the right size for its location. Known as 555 Kelly, the proposal includes 39 income-restricted apartments and one manager’s unit at 535–555 Kelly Ave. The city lists the estimated cost at $41.6 million. Half Moon Bay’s City Council adopted the ordinance approving the agreements with Mercy Housing on May 5. But opponents gathered enough signatures to force a referendum. A yes vote would uphold the ordinance, including a 99-year ground lease at $1 a year. A no vote would reject it. The measure requires a simple majority to pass. If Measure Q fails, the ordinance would not take effect, and the council could not reenact it for one year, according to the city. Belinda Hernandez-Arriaga leads Ayudando Latinos A Soñar, or ALAS, the nonprofit partnering with Mercy Housing on the project. “We have seniors here from 60 and into their 80s working in the field, believe it or not,” she said. Hernandez-Arriaga said farmworkers live in a patchwork of accommodations, including employer-provided housing that charges rent, barracks, trailers, campers and small spaces shared with other families. Some live in their cars, she said. The proposed development would pair apartments with community space and support services. State Sen. Josh Becker, who secured $2 million in state funding for the project, said the 2023 Half Moon Bay mass shooting exposed substandard living conditions at farms. For senior farmworkers who have spent decades doing physically demanding work, Becker said, the development offers a chance for a “safe, dignified retirement.” He also pointed to its proximity to health services and a church as reasons the location makes sense. Opponents say the project’s height could change the downtown’s character. Hal Bogner, who helped organize the referendum through Let Half Moon Bay Voters Decide, said the dispute is about whether the city will remain a place of three-story buildings or move toward taller developments. Opponents also cite traffic, safety and the plan for only 18 on-site parking spaces. They dispute the transit designation used to justify a fifth floor under state density-bonus law. Former Mayor Mike Ferreira said an earlier proposal was only for a four-story building. He criticized the approval of a fifth floor, questioning the transit designation used to justify the added height. Hernandez-Arriaga said the extra height made more sense economically and was not much taller than a building across the street from 555 Kelly Ave. The financing plan relies on county and state grants and loans, along with tax credits, according to the city. Opponents question whether Half Moon Bay could face future costs. Becker emphasized that the project draws on state affordable housing programs. “It’s not funded locally,” he said. “It’s money from the state, it’s money for affordable housing programs.” Under the agreements, Mercy Housing would be responsible for constructing and maintaining the development. It must also meet financing and other predevelopment conditions before entering into the ground lease, according to the city attorney’s impartial analysis. The San Mateo County Farm Bureau opposes the project, arguing that many farmworkers want to live where they work. Bureau President BJ Burns said he houses seven families and that most of his workers want to remain on the farm.”They wanna live where they’re working. The majority of them wanna stay where they’re working”, he said. Longtime flower grower Louie Figone, the bureau’s vice president, said he has been upgrading housing on his property and installing new units. Jeff Regan, an officer with the Yes on Measure Q campaign, questions whether farm owners’ opposition is partly financial, suggesting they see the project as competition for the rental housing they provide at their farms. After opposing the Mercy Housing lease in May, Mayor Debbie Ruddock suggested that the county consider directing money equivalent to the project’s first five years of rent subsidies toward immediate housing on farms. Ruddock, who is seeking reelection, was unavailable for an interview for this report. Both sides point to Stone Pine Cove, an affordable homeownership community built with state funding after the mass shooting, as a successful example of farmworker housing. The ballot fight comes as Half Moon Bay faces a state lawsuit over its housing-planning obligations. Attorney General Rob Bonta and the California Department of Housing and Community Development announced the case in July, alleging the city had failed to comply with state Housing Element Law. That law requires local governments to plan for their share of regional housing needs. Approving 555 Kelly would not, by itself, settle that broader case. Nor would a yes vote mean immediate construction. Mercy Housing’s posted schedule anticipates a tax-credit application and construction start in 2027, completion in 2029 and full occupancy in 2030. Those dates are projections. For Rosales, it all comes back to the family he wants to bring under one roof. He described his hope in Spanish: the three of them living together, coming home in peace and having a place to rest.

headlines.title: 2 San Jose police officers arrested, charged after internal investigation
headlines.description: Two San Jose police officers were arrested and charged with evidence tampering and filing a false police report, the department announced Thursday. Raydarius Surry, 29, and Destiney Thompson, 30, are accused of confiscating drugs from someone on the street to replace drug evidence that was lost in another case, according to police. The two are in a relationship and have been with the department for several years – eight for Surry and six for Thompson. Back in August, police launched an investigation into Surry in connection with an arrest he made on May 3. Surry was notified by the department in August that a small baggie containing a small amount of suspected narcotics, which had been listed in his police report, was never booked into evidence, according to police. The baggie was slated to be tested by the county crime lab. On Aug. 12, after being told about the missing evidence, Surry stopped a pedestrian unrelated to the May 3 case and found a similar baggie of suspected narcotics, police said. Surry seized the baggie, did not take any additional enforcement action and later booked the baggie into evidence under the May 3 case number. He did not document the Aug. 12 stop or evidence seizure. Police said Thompson watched body camera footage of the May 3 arrest to allegedly help Surry formulate a plan to replace the missing evidence. “When you take that careless mistake and you conspire to cover it up and plant evidence and create a false police report, now you’re talking about a felony and tremendous erosion of public trust in the department,” legal analyst Steven Clark said. Surry and Thompson surrendered late Wednesday evening and were booked into county jail, police said. They later posted bail and were no longer in custody as of Thursday evening. “Officers are required to maintain the chain of custody without exception and to be completely truthful in their accounts of interactions with the public,” San Jose police Chief Paul Joseph said in a statement. “Falsifying evidence or police reports is a crime, and our Department moved swiftly to remove both officers from duty and pursue criminal accountability. These allegations, if proven to be true, constitute a failure to live up to the standards our community has a right to expect. I will not tolerate any Department member violating the sacred trust placed in us.” Surry was placed on paid administrative leave on Sept. 2 while the investigation was underway, according to police. Thompson was placed on paid administrative leave on Sept. 18. Investigators are conducting a thorough review of both officers’ cases, arrests and evidence bookings, the department said. No other discrepancies have been found so far. Silicon Valley De-Bug, a police watchdog group, said the case impacts the department’s credibility. “This is affirming to those that have said that police are not infallible and that they do lie and that they do make up evidence, they plant evidence,” Silicon Valley De-Bug organizer Raj Jayadev said. In a statement, the San Jose Police Officers’ Association said it was deeply disappointed, writing, “If proven true, their actions run counter to the level of honesty and integrity necessary to wear our uniform. The POA will not fund their legal defense…” SJPD referred the case to the California Commission on Peace Officer Standards and Training for temporary decertification review, police said. The police department’s Criminal Investigations Detail referred the criminal investigation to the Santa Clara County District Attorney’s Office, which filed charges Wednesday afternoon.

headlines.title: Family of boy with autism wins countersuit against neighbor in San Jose
headlines.description: A neighbor sued a San Jose family whose son has autism, claiming the child’s grunts in the backyard were a “nuisance.” The family countersued and, this week, a jury ruled in their favor. Ezequiel, known as Zeke, is a 14-year-old teenager who suffers from Level 3 autism, a severe form of the disorder that sometimes involves loud grunting. “It requires very high support needs – usually full care with dressing, bathing, toileting, dangers, safety,” Zeke’s mom Serena Arvayo said. “It’s a lot.” Zeke and his mom lived with her dad in a home in San Jose until a neighbor filed a lawsuit, claiming her property value was dropping because of Zeke, and that she was suffering emotional distress, labeling the child a “nuisance.” That’s a word the family says traumatized them. “It was very hurtful,” Arvayo said. “You use that for maybe an animal or a car alarm that won’t go off, but not an autistic individual.” “Completely outrageous,” said Elizabeth Hansen with Behar Gibbs Savage Paulson, LLP. I mean, how can a family intentionally inflict emotional distress on a neighbor because their child was innocently playing in the backyard and making sounds, sounds of joy?” Arvayo says it took away Zeke’s humanity. They moved out of her dad’s rental home so as to not cause more problems, but the neighbor’s lawsuit remained in place. Arvayo then countersued and both suits went to trial. “It’s a challenge,” Arvayo said. “We can’t just live anywhere. Apartments, we won’t live in. Sharing walls is very difficult because we’re always very paranoid about and mindful too of other people, but I always now go next door and say, ‘Hey, this is my son. If you have any issues, please come talk to me.'” This week, the Arvayo family won the countersuit. The jury awarded them $8 million. Arvayo says it gave her son his humanity back. “My son was represented with dignity, and that was the most important thing for him, to have the dignity he deserves,” Arvayo said. “I think the jury in this case was sending a message that in a civilized society, we need to have empathy and compassion and civility at its most basic level,” Arvayo’s lawyer, Missy Cornejo, said. “This sends a message to people that think they can get away with bad behavior,” Arvayo’s lawyer, Ron Rossi, said. “You better be careful because you might pay the consequences.” Repeated messages to the plaintiff’s lawyer have not been returned. The Arvayo family now is relieved, hoping Zeke has given other children on the spectrum a voice.

headlines.title: Homes across the Bay Area report thefts of Halloween decorations
headlines.description: This October, thieves are going after Halloween decorations outside of people’s homes around the Bay Area. A surveillance video in San Francisco shows someone in a green hoodie walking by. He seems to spot the inflatables. He grabs them and then walks away with them. “My husband said, ‘Hey, did you move the blow ups inside for any reason into the garage?’ and I said, ‘No, I didn’t,’ he said, ‘I was going to turn them on but I just looked at the Ring camera and someone came at 2 a.m. and grabbed them’,” SF resident Diana Naranjo said. Naranjo says it happened about a week ago. The decorations were her kids’ favorites. “I was like, ‘Oh man, my boys are going to be disappointed’,” she said. “They were the boys specific favorites because it’s Nightmare Before Christmas. It’s our favorite movie, we couldn’t find a replacement.” And she’s not alone. Last week, NBC Bay Area reported about a San Leandro family who said they got their animatronics stolen. There have also been posts online about stolen decorations along the Peninsula and in San Jose. One neighbor posted on social media a few days ago that their animatronic witch was taken from her front yard in Willow Glen. “What these folks do with it really varies, sometimes you have kids who take things just to take things, you have individuals who vandalize things just to vandalize things and now that we’ve evolved into more high tech equipment for both Halloween and Christmas, we’re going to see an uptick in those thefts because they’re highly sale-able,” law enforcement analyst and retired San Jose Police Detective Michael Leininger said. Neighborhoods all over the Bay Area are known for their spooky decor. Now, many neighbors say they take precautions and have cameras keeping a watchful eye over their yards. Experts say that is exactly what they should do. “If they have surveillance cameras, put up a sign that says you’re under surveillance, people do take those seriously,” Leininger said. Last year, theft was also a problem around Christmas. Leininger says these types of incidents can be low priority for law enforcement agencies, but having those cameras can help.

headlines.title: Dog dies after being attacked by two other dogs near Oakland's Lake Merritt
headlines.description: An Oakland woman is speaking out after her dog died following an attack by two other dogs near Lake Merritt on Oct. 23. For 12 years, Pepper was more than just a pet to Tomiquia Moss. She was family. “When your pet grows up with you, they teach you, they are at your every beck and call, they walk with you in the kitchen, they go to the bathroom with you,” Moss said. But a walk near Oakland’s Lakeside Park last Friday changed everything. “That presence is really difficult to have on a Friday morning. You’re walking your dog and then she’s gone,” she said. On Oct. 23, Moss says two large cane corsos ran towards Pepper and violently attacked her, leaving the dog with serious injuries. “They had her entire body, both dogs, shaking her body for at least three minutes before the man go there,” Moss said. Pepper later died from those injuries and Moss claims the dogs’ owner walked away without showing remorse. “This man who had these animals off leash, watched them maul my dog left the scene,” she said. After a witness shared news of the attack online, other dog owners came forward claiming similar encounters with what they believe were the same dogs. Oakland police and animal services confirm they’re investigating reported dog attacks at city parks but have not confirmed any connection between the incidents. Now Moss wants the owner to be held accountable. “I know that this person will be held accountable and there will be justice for Pepper,” she said.

headlines.title: Having kids out of the question for many Bay Area residents due to high cost of living
headlines.description: The cost of living in the Bay Area is keeping many couples from starting a family, according to a recent survey. Of the roughly 1,800 childless adults younger than 50 surveyed by Joint Venture Silicon Valley, with the Bay Area News Group, 56% said they are unlikely to have children and 58% said they can’t afford to raise kids in the Bay Area. “The screaming headline is that people feel hammered in the Bay Area,” Joint Venture Silicon Valley President and CEO Russell Hancock said. “They can’t afford to live here, and it’s getting worse. The main thing that’s upsetting to folks is that housing seems like it’s now completely out of reach.” NBC Bay Area’s Christie Smith has more in the video report above.
